subtitle: Running a discussion, and interrupting politely
words.intro: Germans love a *Talkshow*, even though they complain about it all week. There are five guests in a half circle, an hour and a question nobody can answer. The real work is done by the person in the middle, who has about three sentences, and uses them to stop people.

grammar[0].fact: The hardest word for a presenter to say in German is nothing at all. Silence puts pressure on the guest, and most guests can’t take it. Try it: ask a short question, and count to four. In this way, you can also get an answer from a teenager.

grammar[1].blocks[2].text: *Bis wann?* is the shortest question in German politics, and very often the one with the longest answer.
grammar[1].fact: German politicians have a word for the talk of a good moderator: *hart, aber fair*. It was the name of a real show. Long panels on Sunday evenings have shaped the political debate here for decades, and viewers count the interruptions.

document.intro: The real first issue of a German radio magazine, from September 1924, when radio was almost brand new. Read how it opens: *Warum? Wieso? Wozu?* It’s three short questions, and then a stop. The editor was a natural presenter.
document.fact: German radio began in October 1923, and it was the talk of the country within a year. Listeners really had to pay a licence fee, as they do today. And *Empfangsstörungen*, interference, were the main topic in the first issues. Nobody had any idea yet what you might actually say on it.

reading.intro: A local TV station has a new talk show, *Klartext*. Tonight’s question: *Mülltrennung: Pflicht oder Wahnsinn?* Max is the presenter, as the real one has flu. In the half circle: Dr. Blum, for the business club; a professor; a Green councillor; and Frau Huber, as a citizen. There are 45 minutes, and Max has cards.

reading.fact: German waste separation is real and intricate: yellow for packaging, blue for paper, brown for food waste, black for the rest, and bottle banks by colour. There are deposits on many bottles, too, so people return them to machines at the supermarket. In some towns, a neighbour may really tell you.
